scope: Explicitly dated, recoverable concrete record findings, supported factual corrections, reviewed relationship assessments and selected working family connections. Dates and explicit date ranges are research retrieval, supplied-record review, original-reading or explicitly dated relationship-review dates stated in maintained evidence, not historical event dates or file modification. Entries based on earlier checked readings identify that reuse and do not imply fresh original inspection. Selected uncertain links retain their individual probabilities, dependencies, alternatives and prior assessment; record-defined kinship is distinguished from adult identity. Undated conclusions, pure confirmations, unselected speculative parent rankings, negative searches and routine profile/build activity are excluded. This is a recoverable dated history, not an exhaustive account of all past research.

findings.finding: The Larne session minutes naming John Glasgow, sen., Robert Glasgow and James Glasgow belong to 1700 and 1701, not 1699 and 1700. John and Robert were stipend bondsmen for Kilwaughter and the South Side on 17 May 1700; James was made overseer for Kilwaughter probably on Thursday 29 May 1701.

He corrects the stipend run to 1700 himself and the weekdays confirm it; the 1701 date for James is an inference from the weekdays. The minutes state no relationship between the three men. No live WikiTree change.

findings.finding: Four original-checked Belfast News-Letter passages from 1840 name Rev. Adam Glasgow: as officiant at a James and Margaret Small marriage, as opening a Townsend-street Presbyterian soirée, among speakers at the Belfast Town Mission annual meeting, and among two Synod ministers accepted for India mission service with James Carr. The Synod report says Kathiawar or Guzerat was selected and gives a planned 4 August departure overland to Bombay.
findings.qualification: The notices give no middle name or unique identifier; the ministerial context is compatible with, but does not uniquely identify, Glasgow-1781. “Wednesday evening last” for the Town Mission meeting is retained as printed. The August journey is planned, not proof of departure. The separate Synod passage names James Carr, not James Glasgow, and establishes no kinship. The 1842 Nancy marriage notice is not included here because the same fact was already documented; it is added only as primary-source corroboration.

daniel-glasco.assessment: Daniel Glasco/Glascow, Norfolk planter, and his wife Mary conveyed 100 acres from Henry Slade’s 330-acre patent to Richard Linton. The upper endorsement expressly says Daniel came into court and acknowledged the act on 3 September 1729, proving him alive then. Daneill Glasco and Richard Linton also witnessed Richard Johnson’s will dated 26 February 1729/30; McIntosh’s abstract is printed page 122. Glasgow-3322, Mary Gamon’s husband in 1693, remains compatible, but the two estates have no proved continuous title chain.

mary.assessment: Mary is expressly Daniel Glasco’s wife in the 1729 deed. Gammon-934 remains compatible with the 1693 John Gamon will’s daughter Mary, wife of Daniel Glasco. Her guessed 1699 death and inconsistent imported spouse field are unsupported and do not exclude her. The 1693 record proves that earlier Mary’s father, but no record yet proves that the 1729 wife is the same woman. Keep the candidate and the lifetime identity qualification together.

richard-linton.assessment: Richard Linton purchased the 1729 land and witnessed Richard Johnson’s will dated 26 February 1729/30 with Daneill Glasco. Linton-898 remains compatible: its estimated 1680 birth, missing death and sparse Virginia family context supply no concrete conflict. Linton-931 also remains a weaker compatible candidate because its 1722 birth is GEDCOM-derived. Linton-494 has cited Lancaster death/probate in 1665, a concrete conflict with the 1729 transaction. Keep the candidate; cite McIntosh’s printed page 122 and do not infer survival to probate.

william-sneddon.assessment: The fresh 1860 index identifies William Sneddon, age 45, widower and collier, with parents Robert Sneddon and Mary Gray Sneddon. james-glasgow.assessment: The live biographies identify two distinct adult Larne men: James Glasgow-1509, ropemaker (1737–1802), and James Glasgow-3991, probable tanner (about 1748–1812). Both survived until the 1779 lease. The separate 1768 messuage names a ropemaker party and a farmer witness, whose roles require separate comparison. Glasgow-1509 is the leading compatible party. No source names the farmer witness's relatives or identifies the 1779 lessee. The 1832 renewal does not establish Anne or Jane as James’s daughters. Keep the 1768 ropemaker party, farmer witness and 1779 lessee roles separate. Jane, wife of Glasgow-3991, died in 1820 and cannot be the 1832 lessee.

anne-glasgow.assessment: Ann Glasgow-3992, born about 1768, died on 25 May 1832 at Larne and was alive on the 25 February 1832 renewal date. Jane, wife of Glasgow-3991, died in 1820 and cannot be the 1832 lessee.

david-mathy.assessment: David Mathy and Mergaret Androsoune, expressly his spouse, bought a barn at Powdrait, Glasgow, on 3 February 1550/51. David Mathy and Robert Glesgw were expressly fellow burgesses witnessing a sasine on 10 May 1554; David also witnessed an act on 4 July 1554. The name and city make the purchaser and witness probably the same man, but the later acts do not repeat the spouse. No kinship with Robert is stated. David Matthew-330 is a weak compatible variant candidate: its only 1701 death assertion is GEDCOM-derived, so it cannot be excluded. The complete sourced draft remains on HOLD against that candidate, with purchaser/witness identity qualified.

david-mathy.assessment: David Mathy and Mergaret Androsoune, expressly his spouse, bought a barn at Powdrait, Glasgow, on 3 February 1550/51. David Mathy and Robert Glesgw were expressly fellow burgesses witnessing a sasine on 10 May 1554; David also witnessed an act on 4 July 1554. The name and city make the purchaser and witness probably the same man, but the later acts do not repeat the spouse. No kinship with Robert is stated. David Matthew-330 is a weak compatible variant candidate: its only 1701 death assertion is GEDCOM-derived, so it cannot be excluded. The complete sourced draft remains on HOLD against that candidate, with purchaser/witness identity qualified.

margaret-androsoune.assessment: Mergaret Androsoune is expressly David Mathy’s spouse in the 3 February 1550/51 Glasgow barn purchase. No age, birthplace, parents, children or death is stated. Anderson-3241 is a sparse compatible candidate with unknown dates, Scotland locality and an unsupported John Kelman spouse; no record proves identity or a conflict. The spouse clause is certain for the documentary couple, while her existing-profile identity remains unresolved.

findings.finding: Selected an uncertain Ayrshire-to-Maryland route through the existing 1679 Kilwinning John comparison and the 1700 West Kilbride Patrick childhood; retained all accounts and the conflicting birth estimates separately.
findings.qualification: Two uncertain father hypotheses are selected; both depend on unproved child/adult identities. Their combination is a conditional model, not two independent confirmations of an Ayrshire-to-Maryland descent. The corresponding child and adult accounts are retained separately without a merge; connectivity counts retained profile accounts rather than proved distinct people. No original parish image, new kinship clause, certain relationship upgrade, mother assignment or live WikiTree save is claimed. Current vital fields and confidently marked relationships are preserved, with the conflicting estimates explicitly explained. John Glasgow-551, associated with County Tyrone in the William Melanchthon Glasgow family account, remains an alternative identity already named on the West Kilbride profile. His estimated birth and the absence of a West Kilbride event do not exclude him. The Ayrshire comparison is preferred for its specific neighbouring parishes and independently indexed 1679 child, not because an Irish route has been disproved. Another local John, a brother or cousin of the Kilwinning family, or a different father remains possible. The Kilwinning-child/Stevenston-adult identity is itself uncertain. No occupation, later residence or marriage connects John-3161 to either adult. Barbara Alason/Allason is named with the 1679 child; no mother is selected for the West Kilbride account, and Margaret Cowan is not assigned as Patrick’s mother from the later Stevenston events. John-3375’s earlier family scaffold retains its existing uncertainty. The Gordon Patrick Glasgow-1440, indexed in 1667 and associated with Helen Fairburn and a later Scottish family, remains an alternative childhood/adult comparison. He would have been about sixty-eight at James’s 1735 birth and sixty-nine at the 1736 ordination if baptised near birth: less economical than the 1700 route, but not an exclusion. The Maryland-linked Patrick Glasgow-3002 is another unresolved account; its unsupported 1720 birth estimate does not identify or exclude him as the minister, and its cited Treasury entry has not been newly interpreted here. Other unrecorded Scottish or Irish childhoods remain possible. The 1700 child’s later life and the minister’s pre-1736 life are untraced. Shared forename, surname and plausible ages are indirect evidence, not a parent clause. Mary Jones remains the minister’s recorded wife; no new marriage, mother, migration date or Scottish parish of birth is asserted.

findings.finding: Selected James Glasgow-3332 as uncertain father of the Carnwath/Libberton Robert Glasgow-3407 through the possible Lindsaylands-weaver identity; an earlier Robert birth is required. The overlapping Gibson/Watson Robert remains separate, with his existing Johne father unchanged.
findings.qualification: One new uncertain father is selected from existing index and family reviews. The 1680 weaver identity and an earlier Robert birth are required conditions; no new original inspection, certain relationship upgrade, mother assignment, identity merge or live WikiTree save is claimed. Existing vital fields and confidently marked metrics are unchanged. The two Robert accounts remain separate retained profiles, and no genealogical certainty is inferred from their inclusion in one working family. The Carnwath marriage citation gives Robert and Katherine Wilson in 1713; the captured 1722 Libberton baptism citation names Robert and Katharin Wilson as John’s parents. Those index citations define the proposed Wilson household but supply no paternal ancestry or age for Robert. The neighbouring Robert Glasgow-4168 account combines Katherin Gibson in 1718 and Katherine Watson in 1720 and 1726. The Wilson event in 1722 falls between the Watson events. Consequently, a simple sequence of remarriages does not reconcile all maternal surnames. Transcription differences, record misassignment, overlapping families, or one man across some entries remain possible. No woman is equated with another, and no new marriage or mother is assigned. The two Robert accounts are retained separately; shared parish and forename do not prove identity. Johne Glasgow-3093 remains an unselected alternative father for the Carnwath Robert, particularly if Robert Glasgow-3407 is eventually identified with the Gibson/Watson Robert Glasgow-4168, whose selected father is already Johne. Johne’s birth around 1648 could fit fatherhood around 1690; however, no later record follows him from the Mid Calder child entry to Libberton. Giving him both Roberts would otherwise require two living sons with the same forename or an unproved identity between the accounts. The present choice avoids building that assumption into the default model. If James Glasgow-3332’s two father assignments and the Johne Glasgow-3093 to Robert Glasgow-4168 choice are right, Robert Glasgow-3407 would be the latter Robert’s paternal uncle. That is a consequence of the conditional model, not independent evidence of kinship. Another unrecorded local father and a younger Lindsaylands generation remain possible. Captain Robert Glasgow-2867 also remains a surviving identity comparison; his unsupported imported family is not a concrete exclusion, and no maritime or probate bridge identifies the Carnwath man with him.

relationship_changes.explanation: Prefer one household: James Glasgow, indexed with Agnes Waitte at Polwarth on 18 June 1663, is probably the James who fathered the Gordon children John (1666), Patrike (1667), Jean (1671), Robert (1673), Agnes (1676) and Margrat (1679). The father’s repeated full name, the neighbouring Berwickshire parishes, the first child three years after marriage and the orderly thirteen-year child sequence form a coherent family. The daughter Agnes supplies modest naming support; it is not the deciding evidence. The maintained 1702 Gordon marriage citation for Jean also names father James, adding a compatible adult continuation for her. Read together, these favour a single local family over six isolated fathers or an unrelated Polwarth couple. No concrete competing contemporary Gordon James household has been identified in the maintained material. That is the scope of this comparison, not a claim to have exhausted the population. The child indexes explicitly name James as father but omit the mother. Their named-father roles are documented for the record-defined children; identifying that father with the 1663 Polwarth husband is probable. Agnes Watt is separately assessed as probable mother of all six children on the marriage, locality and sustained family sequence. This is an inference, not literal maternity in the indexes; a later marriage or another local James remains possible. Jean’s later marriage and the later adult identities of John and Patrick remain separately assessed. Patrick’s proposed Kilclone son and migration, James’s own John Glasgow-1084 ancestry and the unrelated Kilwaughter James are not strengthened. No original register image was newly inspected: this review combines the previously accepted index entries and maintained citations.

findings.finding: The Whitecastle James was reported imprisoned in July 1672, not fined in 1670. The printed decree and named Biggar-area neighbours support a probable Libberton setting. A conditional uncertain father in the existing Quothquan family is now selected through the possible Lindsaylands identity.
findings.qualification: The printed decree in Robert Wodrow’s 1721 History, volume I, appendix no. XLVII, pp.133–134, is dated 27 July 1672 in both its heading and Latin opening. It names “James Glasgow in Whitecastle” among people imprisoned for refusing the oath. The monetary fines there belong to Mr James Duncan and the Countess of Wigtoun, not to James Glasgow. William Crookshank’s 1751 summary, volume I p.285, places the same named group under 24 July 1672; preserve that day discrepancy and prefer the printed decree’s 27 July for this source account. Neither source supports the old 1670 date. The two books recount the same proceeding and are not independent evidence of two imprisonments. The surrounding Biggar/Boghall group names men in Biggar, Carwood, Edmonstoun, Worslyd and Carstairs. This favours the Whitecastle in Libberton parish over a location guessed merely from general Covenanter activity. J. L. Davidson’s published article title locates West Whitecastle Farm in Libberton, Lanarkshire (Proceedings of the Society of Antiquaries of Scotland 108, p.383; title checked in the journal’s search-indexed contents, full article not inspected). This supports the Libberton place identification, in the same parish setting as Quothquan and near Biggar’s Lindsaylands; it does not identify a seventeenth-century occupier. This is a probable interpretation of James’s residence, not a parish supplied literally by the decree. White Castle in Garvald and Bara, East Lothian, is a real alternative place. The decree also deals with a Perthshire group; document order alone does not put every accused person in Clydesdale. There are two dependent gaps: Whitecastle James is not proved to be the Lindsaylands weaver, and John’s paternity of James-3332 is itself unproved. John’s 1685 Quothquan testament names his widow but no child; the absence of James, if dead by 1680, would not exclude this model. James-3332’s possible identity with the 1624 weaver would invalidate this particular later-life route, because the 1624 decedent cannot be the man present in 1672. James-1150, the Edinburgh weaver, remains an alternative adult identification for the later weaver rather than being excluded from an unsupported birth estimate; another local James or a different kinship degree remains possible. The old Marion-baptism role error supplies no positive parentage for James-1376, and the Duffe household James-2682 is not merged. The 1738 Edinburgh Castle lead is unselected and incompatible with a death by 1680 if this weaver identity is right. No 1680 original was newly read: the maintained case has only the supplied wills index, and no linked manuscript or transcription. Neither a marriage nor a mother is supplied. Jonet Kinnie, John’s widow, is not automatically James’s mother. Keep both James profiles separate; they may represent one man, not two proved brothers. The fixed historical cohort and all names, dates, places, spouses, existing father choices and live WikiTree fields are preserved. The circa-1650 birth on James-1376 is an estimate; the newly checked occurrence is in 1672, not a pre-1650 record. One selected uncertain father connects this previously isolated account locally. Supported and confident paternal measurements remain unchanged. Working counts concern retained profile accounts and may include the unresolved duplicate represented by the two James profiles; a gained connection is not another proved person or a proved pedigree. The 27/24 July discrepancy and imprisonment-versus-fine correction remain visible beside the family hypothesis.

findings.finding: John of Kirkliston is placed provisionally under Thomas Glasgow and Janet Mill, each at 42%, through the possible 1750 Mid Calder child identification.
findings.qualification: Select Thomas Glasgow-1023 and Janet Mill-357 as possible working parents of John Glasgow-159, each at 42%, conditional on the Kirkliston husband being the John represented by Glasgow-2980 at Mid Calder in 1750. The Mid Calder account already identifies that named couple. A man recorded in 1750 could marry in 1785 at about 35 and father the Kirkliston children in 1786–1797. The catalogue’s circa-1761 birth for the husband is an unsupported estimate, not an age that excludes him. Mid Calder/Livingston and Kirkliston form a compatible Lothian labouring-family route. The first recorded son Thomas (1786) and later daughter Janet (1790) repeat both proposed parents’ names, giving this couple a modest positive advantage over the other local John households. The identifying step is an inference: no inspected record takes the 1750 child to Kirkliston or names the husband’s parents. The Thomas/Janet naming fit is supporting context, not a compulsory naming rule or two independent proofs. John-3581 (Kirknewton 1755, John/Mary Robertson), John-3480 (Kirknewton/East Calder 1751, John/Christian Meek) and John-2846 (West Calder 1747, John/Margaret Anderson) all remain compatible. Their blank later lives do not exclude them. John-1304’s estimated 1771 childhood and Muckle household make him a weaker comparison, without proving that the estimate or any first-marriage assumption is right. Another unindexed John remains possible. The 1750 FamilySearch index citations were reused from maintained captures; this review reached the provider’s sign-in page and did not inspect the original register. The two index URLs refer to one event, not independent corroboration. John-2980 and John-159 remain separate accounts that may represent one man; the selected parents do not establish two distinct sons named John. The husband’s birth field stays circa 1761, explicitly unproved, until identity is resolved. Thomas’s Kilwinning childhood and the family’s earlier ancestry are separate inherited identifications and are not strengthened. The same 42% applies to each parent because both depend on that one child-to-adult identity; these are not independent probabilities. One new working paternal edge; no confident-edge gain, discovered parent clause, live edit or identity merge.

findings.finding: Robert Glasgow, Margaret Brash’s husband, has selected probable parents James Glasgow and Marion Saidler, 62% each, through the older widower and 1760 baptism identification.
findings.qualification: Robert Glasgow-1538, Margaret Brash’s husband, is probably the older widower represented by Robert Glasgow-1530. Both accounts claim the same Barony marriage, 6 November 1803, OPR 622/70/252. The older account has a coherent local sequence: marriage to Elizabeth Jack in 1789, her death or burial in 1802, marriage to Margaret Brash in 1803, and a Glasgow weaver’s burial or death in 1839 aged 79. That age favours the Robert baptised at Wandell and Lamington on 17 February 1760, whose indexed parents are James Glasgow and Marion Saidler, over the 1755, 1758 and 1784 births. James Glasgow-1120 and Marion Sadler-2849 are therefore selected as probable working parents of Robert-1538, at 62% each. The two profiles’ identical marriage citation is one event claimed twice, not independent proof that the men are identical. Neither the child-to-adult bridge nor the linkage of the 1839 weaver to the groom has been proved. The 1758 Livingston child of Abraham Glasgow and Janet Cunnyngham, the 1755 Mid Calder child of Andrew Glasgow and Janet Young, and the 1784 Glasgow child remain compatible alternatives; burial ages may be approximate. Robert-2963 and the James Glasgow-1142/Jean Simpson family remain a weaker derivative-tree comparison, not an excluded family. Robert-1538 and Robert-1530 remain separate accounts that may represent one adult, not evidence of two sons with the same name. The local working birth is now before the 17 February 1760 baptism, explicitly a probable identity rather than an exact birthday. The captured WikiTree 13 September 1784 value is retained in the comparison and as a competing child record; no live date was changed. The 62% assessments concern the 1760 named-parent roles; James-1120’s identification with the 1738 child and his earlier ancestry remain separate inherited uncertainties. Marion is assessed from the named mother in the baptism, not inferred solely from James’s spouse. Both percentages depend on the same identity chain and are not independent probabilities. This review reuses maintained index citations and earlier contributors’ readings; no original register image was newly inspected. Alexander-2822’s 1861 marriage names Robert and Margaret, but does not identify Robert’s parents. Ralph-1537 and the other attached children are not strengthened by this selection; the 1819 Janet Gilmour groom remains unproved. One new probable paternal edge; no new original-source discovery or confident-edge gain.

findings.finding: The 1779 Eccles marriage and an earlier James child clarify Robert Glasgow’s Leitholm household. James Glasgow of Stichill is selected as a possible working father at 34%.
findings.qualification: Select James Glasgow (Glasgow-1238), the father recorded with Elizabath/Elizabeth Tait at Stichill, as Robert Glasgow’s possible working father, at 34%. The couple’s maintained marriage citation is dated 25 January 1740; their David and James children are indexed in June 1744 and July 1746. Robert’s estimated 1745 birth fits that family generation and could fall between those events; it is not a dated baptism. Stichill and Eccles/Leitholm belong to the same small Borders district, and the later Swinton entry attributed to the James/Tait couple offers a further local comparison. Robert’s earlier son James supplies a modest naming clue consistent with this father; a common forename cannot establish paternity. The combination favours this existing, record-defined family over the catalogue’s distant Kirknewton candidates, whose apparent proximity came from mapping Leitholm to South Leith. No inspected record names Robert as James’s son. This is a preferred, revisable hypothesis, with 34% subjective confidence, not a measured probability or a confident connection. Robert’s 1745 birth and 8 August 1800 death each have zero attached sources on the inspected FamilySearch tree. Neither date establishes an age or place of birth. The local 1745 estimate is retained unchanged. FamilySearch attaches John Glasgow (1720–1785, GFNP-FS8) and Agnes Spark (1722–deceased, K8CD-HCW) as parents; retain that alternative without treating a contributed tree as documentary proof. The evidential basis of that parent attachment has not yet been reviewed. Do not equate that John with the much older John Glasgow-1057, husband of Agnes Spark-330, from the matching names alone. James’s brother John Glasgow-1444, christened at Stichill in 1708, is another compatible local father-generation alternative with no presently inspected Robert link. An unrecorded local father or another kinship degree remains possible. The Swinton/1740 couple continuity and Robert’s own early life need testing. Elizabeth Tait is not selected as Robert’s mother: her marriage and maternity of other children do not identify his mother. Robert is not merged with an earlier child, and James’s existing older ancestry retains its own uncertainty.

findings.finding: The Martinsburg Robert’s cited family tree explicitly reports a John father. The documented 1766 Drumearn householder John Glasgow is selected as a possible working match at 31%.
findings.qualification: The Geneanet entry already cited in Robert’s saved biography was inspected directly. It represents the man reported born in 1769 in Ireland and dead at Martinsburg on 26 November 1858, with the same wife and children. It explicitly attaches John Glasgow, born 1745 in Ireland, and Margaret, entered under the surname Nee, as parents. John’s own page cites only Ancestry Family Trees. This verifies what the contributed tree says; it does not verify historical paternity, either parent’s birth, or Margaret’s surname. The page gives Ireland, not County Tyrone. Robert’s more specific Tyrone origin remains an inherited local-profile claim. Select John Glasco of Drumearn (Glasgow-2990) as Robert Glasgow-1189’s possible working father, at 31% subjective confidence. The specific reported father name John favours a John comparison over the automated leading candidate James Glasgow-1970. The actual 1766 Derryloran return places John at Drumearn beside two James Glasco households, three years before Robert’s estimated birth. That supplies a real Tyrone father-generation account compatible with the reported origin. John’s circa-1750 local estimate and the contributed father’s 1745 year are both unproved; either permits fatherhood around 1769, and no date is changed to fit. The estimate assesses the whole proposition that the documented householder was the reported father. It is not a rating of the census record, a statistical probability, or a product of the uncertain ancestry above John. There are two unresolved steps: whether the contributed John/Margaret parentage is correct, and whether that John was the Drumearn householder. A common given name, estimated generation and claimed county cannot establish identity. The 1766 return supplies no wife, child, age or parent; the nearby James entries do not identify John’s father. Robert’s Tyrone birthplace is not independently established by the inspected Geneanet page. John’s existing uncertain James Glasgow-2988 father is preserved, with no new support. The Cookstown reward subscriber of 1796 is an unresolved namesake comparison, with Robert Glasgow-3941 the stronger maintained candidate; that notice supplies no parent and is not used as proof that the Martinsburg man lived at Cookstown. The single Geneanet/Ancestry family-tree chain and its repetition in WikiTree are not independent witnesses. Retain another unidentified Irish John as a serious alternative. John Glasgow-3314, associated with Margaret Mill and the West Calder children of 1762–1770, matches both reported parental given names and a viable generation, but has no inspected Robert or Irish-origin bridge. His Scottish baptism and actual West Calder household are distinct facts; an unproved Irish birthplace is not a categorical exclusion. John Glasgow-4179 of Larne also fits the estimated generation; his known Rose Allan marriage does not prove there was no earlier Margaret, but no record connects him with Robert or Drumearn. James Glasgow-1970 has a Cookstown family tradition and a rare Julia/Julia Ann descendant-name resemblance; those are useful regional clues, but do not outweigh the specific reported John father name. If that report is wrong, James or another local man remains possible. No competing candidate is rejected merely for missing fields. No mother is selected: the reported Margaret is not identified with Margaret Mill, Rose Allan or any existing profile, and Nee is not adopted as a verified birth surname. Robert’s wife Elizabeth and every existing child remain unchanged. No merge, vital-field change, live WikiTree save or confidence upgrade is made.

findings.qualification: The saved biography of John Glasgow-1549 explicitly reports that he and Margaret Hunter sailed for America in 1781 with two young sons, Richard and John (2), and that William was born during the voyage. Its attached children include Richard, William, Matthew and Taylor Wilson, but no John. This is an overlooked, specific family attribution in a contributed account, not a newly discovered passenger list or inspected birth record. The underlying source of the travel and son statements is not identified. The separate will citation must not be presented as having proved those statements: its image could not be inspected in this review. findings.finding: 200 earliest remaining father links individually rated, for children dated 1792–1825. All 772 selected father links through 1800 now have individual confidence estimates.
findings.qualification: Ratings distinguish named record fathers from unproved childhood-to-adult identifications. The historical citations were already held; one missing profile narrative was refreshed for its complete comparison. No original image was newly inspected. This batch records individual confidence measurements of existing father links; it adds no new fathers or branch joins. Six inherited confident marks are assessed below 90% after their individual evidence and identity limits are reviewed; these decreases are retained.

confidence_reductions.basis: Faris’s 1990 Glasgow Family genealogy places Phoebe among Robert and Rosanna’s ten children and cites her marriage at p.37. Her 1793–1832 memorial and Adams County family agree with the selected Robert.

The held FamilySearch church-index account places Peter Glasgow, 18 March 1808, in John Glasgow and Jean Bryce’s child sequence. The 1841 Hume’s Close household supports that adult family, while identification with the 1783 Bathgate child remains strongly circumstantial.

The held family outline assigns Hugh Glasgow, born 1817, to Alexander, fitting his 1786/1788 generation and Deer Township context. It promises census sources but provides no particular parent-naming extract for this child.

Margaret’s biography calls her Robert Barclay Glasgow and Rosanna Finley’s daughter, describing her 1848 move with cousin Nathaniel Cyrus Patton. Her 1850/1860 censuses and memorial support the adult identity without independently naming her father.

The FamilySearch New Monkland baptism account for Thomas Leishman Glasgow, 6 October 1822, names John Glasgow and Marrion Anderson, fitting their 1810 marriage. John’s identification with the 1790 Kirknewton child remains plausible but unbridged; the Janet household is excluded.

The FamilySearch New Monkland baptism account for William Clark Glasgow, 19 December 1824, names John Glasgow and Marrion Anderson, fitting their 1810 marriage. John’s identification with the 1790 Kirknewton child remains plausible but unbridged; the Janet household is excluded.

findings.finding: 390 earliest remaining father links individually rated, for children dated 1825–1850. All 1,396 currently selected eligible father links through 1850 now have individual confidence estimates.
findings.qualification: Ratings distinguish named record fathers from unproved childhood-to-adult identifications. This uses held evidence and cited profile accounts; one missing profile narrative was refreshed for its complete comparison. No original image was newly inspected. This batch records individual confidence measurements of existing father links; it adds no new fathers or branch joins. 14 inherited confident marks are assessed below 90%; the decreases and prior status evidence are preserved.

findings.finding: William Glasgow’s Currituck will, dated 14 October 1805 and recorded 22 January 1806, names wife Sarah, sons Caleb, Isaac, Samuel and John C., and daughters Ruth, Love Bright and Sophia. Its land divisions and household bequests identify one specific family. The named wife and all seven child names strongly identify the maintained William-357 family, with John C. compatible with John Cooper and Love now recorded under Bright; this conjunction outweighs the unsourced August death claim. The published transcription is by Judy Merrell Brickhouse, citing Currituck County Will Book 2, pp.279–280. The manuscript was not inspected. The will also transfers an enslaved boy; that clause does not add a biological family relationship.
findings.qualification: Seven existing father links become confident; the second Isaac account stays possible at 43% and may be a duplicate, not an eighth named child. No new father attachment or merge. Death is after the will date, not the imported August day; exact death, mothers and older ancestry remain separate.

findings.finding: The published obituary transcription identifies Samuel Steel Glasgow, then in his ninetieth year, as the surviving brother of Stewart Glasgow of Hanna City. The distinctive name and age fit Samuel Steele Glasgow-9, born in September 1814. Stewart’s established Peoria family and independently reviewed 94% paternal identification with Robert Barclay Glasgow-8 support extending the same father to this documented brother. This is a confident combined paternal inference, not a literal statement naming Samuel’s father in the obituary.
findings.qualification: Existing father 58% → 92%, confident; no new father attachment or identity merge. 92% is a subjective assessment of the complete Samuel-9 to Robert-8 father identification. The obituary supplies the sibling relationship; the 1880 county sketch and 1925 family interview comparisons identify Stewart and support his father. The Peoria Star abstract and Monmouth Review account quoting the Peoria Herald Transcript may derive from one obituary and are not counted as independent parentage witnesses. Published transcription inspected; original newspaper image uninspected. Mother and all vital fields remain separately assessed.

relationship_changes.subject: Glasgow-1150
relationship_changes.explanation: The 1641 apprenticeship expressly names Robert as James’s father and supplies the Wester Duddingston association. The 1649 burgess entry repeats William Sclaitter and the exact 16 June 1641 apprenticeship date, securely identifying that son as the Edinburgh weaver James-1150. The indexed Robert Glasgow burial in the same parish on 17 January 1647 is a coherent match to that father six years later. No positively evidenced competing Duddingston Robert has emerged from the held family comparisons. Robert-1027 is a Glasgow cordiner with proved parents but no held Duddingston connection; Robert-4006 is a possible earlier identity of this adult, not evidence of a second local father. Together these positive identity and locality links warrant 91% confident inference rather than retaining a probable ceiling solely for an unattested namesake possibility.
relationship_changes.previous_status_provenance: Robert Glasgow-1156 is now assessed as the probable father of James Glasgow-1150, the Edinburgh weaver. Grant’s 16 June 1641 apprenticeship names James’s father Robert and places the entry at Wester Duddingston with William Crichtoun and master William Sclaitter. The 20 June 1649 burgess admission repeats Sclaitter’s name and the exact apprenticeship date, securely connecting the recorded son to the adult weaver. The Robert buried at Duddingston on 17 January 1647 fits the father’s name, parish and preceding generation, six years after the apprenticeship and before James’s independent household began in 1649. Taken together, the specific local father and the Duddingston burial favour one Robert over an otherwise unattested second contemporary Robert in that parish. The previous assessment treated the lack of a unique identifier as a reason to stop at plausible; the combined argument warrants probable, while remaining an inference.

findings.finding: Actual Faris book inspection corrects five overstated Moneymore father probabilities: Robert85%→35%, Arthur/Joseph82%→35%, John76%→30%, Mary64%→22%.
findings.qualification: The actual Faris book has now been inspected, rather than only its catalogue abstract. Printed p.11 uses a dotted possible connection from James of Moneymore to the American brothers; p.12 explicitly reports that evidence for Robert and his brothers’ parentage had not been found. James was the author’s identifiable County Londonderry candidate, not an evidenced father. The retrospective Irish pedigree on pp.8–9 and Samuel’s 1824 Pennsylvania will discussed on p.12 identify an Irish sibling group, including William, James and Robert remaining in Ireland, without joining it to the emigrant brothers. County setting, a compatible generation and the existing family tradition keep James a plausible candidate, but cannot sustain the earlier probable father assessment. Mary’s case additionally depends on identifying the 1779 will witness Mary Arter as the emigrant sister. Faris p.13 transmits an unnamed sister styled Mrs Arthur; p.15 identifies Mary Arter with that sister through the tax/probate cluster, rather than an explicit sibling or birth statement. The association remains positive but does not establish her father. Robert, Arthur and Joseph’s established brotherhood remains separately supported by the maintained 1806 letter transcription and Joseph’s 1831 will. John of Peters Township remains a probable brother at 83%; Faris p.15 also reconstructs the four brothers from the 1779–1780 tax/probate cluster. These sibling arguments do not identify their father. The 1824 Samuel will has been read only through Faris’s excerpt, not its manuscript. The Irish Robert in that will/pedigree is not identified as the emigrant Robert born in 1749. All mothers, upstream ancestry, life dates and current attachments are preserved; no live WikiTree save or identity merge follows. Exact percentages are subjective pair-specific judgments, not measured frequencies or multiplied probabilities.

The letter-defined father is the family role represented by James-1025. These are specific named relationships, substantially stronger than the contributed-tree and locality summaries used by the earlier percentages. The same full-letter tradition was already read on 20 October; actual Faris pages now confirm its full structure. Its reproduction by Albert Rutherford and Faris’s pedigree are dependent presentations, not independent witnesses. These are probable, not confident, relationships reconstructed from an anonymous retrospective family recollection, with no newly inspected parent register. The original letter remains uninspected. Faris calls the anonymous recollection file5 within PRONI T1959, while Rutherford’s reproduced copy cites T1959/3; retain this reference discrepancy pending archive checking. The 1759 probate index says Drumcarn and names no kin; neither that testator nor the inherited life dates are identified by this reassessment. The letter calls William eldest although the imported sibling birth estimates put him later; those estimates remain unverified. Faris also flags Samuel’s infant daughter and surviving mother-in-law in1824 against the supposed early paternal death. Those tensions require testing, not automatic exclusion. Preserve all existing people, vital fields, maternal grades and alternatives. No Scottish migration, identity merge, live edit or new father attachment is claimed. Existing father links reweighed; no new parent record, new attachment or American-family upgrade.

findings.finding: Samuel Glasgow-2872’s Chester estate is identified;James Glasgow-1025 is the preferred replacement father,67% probable. John-2870 remains25% uncertain alternative,previously 72% probable.
findings.qualification: Samuel-2872 is now identified with the 1824 West Fallowfield testator at 98% subjective confidence: his checked memorial names both wives Judith and Tabitha and the infant daughter Margaret Ellen, matching the original will. The newly inspected official deed index places Samuel in West Fallowfield and enters Judith Heslett in the spouse column in 1805 and 1812, with repeated Haslett dealings. These connect the already recorded Judith household to the later Tabitha estate. The will names the testator’s three brothers William, James and Robert Glasgow of Ireland; the anonymous Irish family recollection names those same three brothers with Samuel, who went to America, as children of James Glasgow and Margaret Rutherford. The distinctive sibling constellation and transatlantic division favour this particular Irish father over the current John reconstruction. The 98% testator identification does not prove his father. 67% is a combined subjective father-profile judgement, not a multiplication of independent probabilities. Repeated family names can occur in another generation. The memorial contributes a 1761 Pennsylvania birth and a John father attribution, but no underlying birth or Bible entry has been inspected. These remain substantive competing claims. The letter account’s estimated 1726 Samuel birth, Margaret Rutherford’s estimated 1700 birth and James’s supposed 1759 death are consequential conflicts if established; no date is adjusted to force the preferred route. The 1759 Drumcarn testator’s identification with James-1025 remains unproved. Samuel-1492 remains the separate letter-defined account, father 76%, with possible duplicate identity, not a proved second son or a merge. Mary Cranmer’s existing maternal attachment is not reassessed or transferred to Margaret Rutherford. The current Find a Grave family links and the compiled Bible narrative are claims, not inspected original parent entries. The deed originals remain unread; Judith Heslett is the index’s spouse-column wording, not an established maiden surname.
